note: On-chain protocol catalog, batch 2: Layer2/scaling, NFT, account abstraction, more DeFi, oracles, interop, consensus, ZK, MEV, signatures, governance, privacy.

protocols.name: Arbitrum Rollup (multi-round fraud proof)
protocols.overview: An optimistic rollup whose dispute game narrows a state assertion over multiple bisection rounds until a single instruction is executed on-chain.

goals.name: assertion_correctness
goals.property: Only correct post-states are confirmed after the dispute game.

goals.name: challenger_liveness
goals.property: An honest challenger can force resolution of a wrong assertion within the timeout.

goals.name: bridge_consistency
goals.property: L1-to-L2 withdrawals follow confirmed state only.

protocols.threat_model: Adversary controls the sequencer and can censor/delay, but at least one honest challenger is live.
protocols.flaw: Safety rests on a live honest challenger within multi-round, multi-day timeouts; censorship of the challenger or an unavailable validator lets a wrong assertion confirm, and forced-inclusion depends on L1 liveness.

protocols.name: OP Stack Optimistic Rollup
protocols.overview: Optimistic rollup with a single-round interactive fault proof (cannon) over an L2 output root, plus a dispute game with a challenger bond.

goals.name: output_root_soundness
goals.property: A challenged invalid output root is rejected.

goals.name: withdrawal_safety
goals.property: Withdrawals cannot release against an invalid root.

goals.name: censorship_resistance
goals.property: Users can force-include deposits via L1.

protocols.threat_model: Adversary is the sequencer and may censor; challenger must be live.
protocols.flaw: Single-round fault proofs rely on a permissioned/live challenger and a finality delay; sequencer censorship and delayed data availability are real attack surfaces (as is the trusted challenge setup).

protocols.name: zkSync Era
protocols.overview: A zkEVM rollup posting state diffs with a validity proof verified on L1; a sequencer orders transactions and a prover generates SNARKs.

goals.name: validity_soundness
goals.property: Only valid state diffs accepted by the verifier are finalized.

goals.name: withdrawal_consistency
goals.property: L1 withdrawals correspond to proven L2 state.

protocols.threat_model: Adversary cannot break the proof system; may censor or withhold data.
protocols.flaw: Correctness reduces to the SNARK soundness and verifier contract; liveness/censorship and data availability are separate, non-soundness concerns.

protocols.name: Starknet (STARK validity rollup)
protocols.overview: A zk rollup using STARK proofs of a Cairo-based state transition, verified on L1, with a sequencer and provers.

goals.name: validity_soundness
goals.property: A state update is accepted only with a valid STARK.

goals.name: state_commitment_binding
goals.property: The proof binds the exact new state root and consumed messages.

protocols.threat_model: Adversary cannot break STARK soundness; sequencer may censor.
protocols.flaw: No soundness flaw given a sound STARK and correct verifier; decentralization/liveness are the open issues.

protocols.name: Scroll zkEVM
protocols.overview: A bytecode-level zkEVM rollup with a proof verifier on L1 and a commit/finalize pipeline.

goals.name: batch_proof_soundness
goals.property: Only batches with valid proofs finalize.

goals.name: message_queue_safety
goals.property: L1<->L2 messages are consumed exactly once.

protocols.threat_model: Adversary cannot forge proofs; may censor and probe message-queue edge cases.
protocols.flaw: No known soundness flaw; message queue and proof verification are the trusted base.

protocols.name: Polygon zkEVM
protocols.overview: A zkEVM rollup with a verification contract, a trusted sequencer, and forced-batch/emergency mechanisms.

goals.name: batch_validity
goals.property: Invalid batches cannot be verified.

goals.name: forced_batch_liveness
goals.property: A user's forced batch is eventually processed.

goals.name: emergency_state_consistency
goals.property: Emergency state transitions cannot steal funds.

protocols.threat_model: Adversary controls/withholds the sequencer; cannot break the proof system.
protocols.flaw: The trusted sequencer plus emergency-state mechanism concentrates power: a malicious/compromised sequencer or admin can delay forced batches or trigger an emergency transition that changes state, and forced-batch liveness can be blocked by gas griefing.

protocols.name: Polygon PoS (checkpoint bridge)
protocols.overview: A PoS sidechain whose checkpoints are submitted to Ethereum by a validator set; an on-chain bridge (Plasma/PoS portal) locks and releases assets.

goals.name: checkpoint_quorum
goals.property: A checkpoint is accepted only with 2/3 validator power.

goals.name: exit_validity
goals.property: Withdrawals require a valid burn proof against a checkpointed root.

protocols.threat_model: Adversary controls <2/3 stake; may exploit exit-proof encoding/validation.
protocols.flaw: The security of the sidechain/bridge is only 2/3 of a permissioned validator set; the bridge has a known history of exit-validation bugs and relies on validators for liveness and safety. Several Polygon-ecosystem bridges were drained.

protocols.name: Loopring zkRollup
protocols.overview: A zkRollup DEX with off-chain order matching and on-chain SNARK-verified settlement; L1 holds funds and verifies batches.

goals.name: settlement_soundness
goals.property: Only valid, operator-signed batches whose proofs verify settle.

goals.name: fund_safety
goals.property: L1 funds cannot be moved except by valid withdrawals.

protocols.threat_model: Adversary may compromise the operator/prover role but cannot break the SNARK.
protocols.flaw: Soundness follows from SNARK verification plus operator signatures; the operator can censor but not steal.

protocols.name: dYdX / StarkEx (validity exchange)
protocols.overview: StarkEx batches off-chain trades and settles with a STARK proof; an on-chain operator manages deposits/withdrawals and a delayed-withdrawal escape hatch.

goals.name: batch_validity
goals.property: Only valid batches with proofs update balances.

goals.name: escape_hatch
goals.property: Users can always withdraw via the on-chain delayed path even if the operator disappears.

protocols.threat_model: Adversary compromises the operator; cannot forge STARK proofs.
protocols.flaw: The STARK + escape-hatch design prevents fund loss under operator failure; availability of the operator is a liveness issue.

protocols.name: Plasma (exit game)
protocols.overview: Plasma chains commit block roots to a parent chain; users exit by a proof and a challenge period during which other users can challenge invalid exits.

goals.name: exit_soundness
goals.property: Only funds the exiting user owns can leave via an exit.

goals.name: mass_exit_safety
goals.property: If the operator withholds data, honest users can still exit.

goals.name: challenge_liveness
goals.property: Invalid exits can be challenged within the period.

protocols.threat_model: Adversary controls the operator and may withhold data or spam exits (exit griefing).
protocols.flaw: Plasma has the known data-availability/exit-griefing problem: an operator can withhold data so honest users cannot prove ownership, and a coalition can flood the exit queue so challenge periods expire; this is why practical systems moved to rollups.

protocols.name: Validium (off-chain data availability)
protocols.overview: A validity proof system where transaction data is kept off-chain (by a committee/DA layer) while only the state root and proof go on-chain.

goals.name: validity_soundness
goals.property: State updates are valid.

goals.name: data_availability
goals.property: All state data is retrievable so users can exit.

protocols.threat_model: Adversary controls the operator/DA committee and may withhold data.
protocols.flaw: Validity does not imply data availability: if the committee withholds data, users cannot reconstruct state or exit with correct balances, so funds can be frozen/stolen even though every proof verifies.

protocols.name: EIP-4844 Proto-Danksharding (blobs)
protocols.overview: Blob-carrying transactions add a KZG commitment to blobs whose data is pruned after ~18 days; rollups use blobs for cheap data availability.

goals.name: kzg_binding
goals.property: A blob's versioned hash binds the exact blob data.

goals.name: proof_soundness
goals.property: Point-evaluation proofs verify against the commitment.

protocols.threat_model: Adversary cannot break KZG; may exploit pruning windows or mempool data withholding.
protocols.flaw: KZG commitments and point-evaluation proofs are binding under the discrete-log assumption; the ~18-day availability window is a design trade-off, not a soundness break.

protocols.name: Celestia Data Availability
protocols.overview: Celestia separates data availability from execution using data-availability sampling and namespaced Merkle trees; rollups post data as blobs and light clients sample.

goals.name: da_soundness
goals.property: A block is accepted only if its data is available under sampling.

goals.name: namespace_binding
goals.property: Data is bound to the correct rollup namespace.

protocols.threat_model: Adversary controls a minority of validators and may attempt unavailable-data attacks; light clients sample.
protocols.flaw: DAS + NMT gives availability guarantees under the sampling assumptions; the known risks are implementation and parameter issues, not a protocol soundness break.

protocols.name: EigenDA (restaked data availability)
protocols.overview: EigenDA uses restaked operators with erasure coding and KZG commitments, where operators attest to storing blobs and can be slashed.

goals.name: blob_availability
goals.property: Committed blobs are retrievable or the responsible operators are slashed.

goals.name: commitment_binding
goals.property: KZG commitments bind the erasure-coded data.

protocols.threat_model: Adversary controls <1/3 restaked stake and may withhold blobs.
protocols.flaw: Availability is enforced by restaked economic security and KZG binding; slashability makes withholding costly.

protocols.name: ERC-721 Non-Fungible Token
protocols.overview: ERC-721 tracks unique token ownership and approves operators via setApprovalForAll; safeTransferFrom calls onERC721Received on contract recipients.

goals.name: ownership_uniqueness
goals.property: A token has exactly one owner and transfers update it atomically.

goals.name: no_unauthorized_transfer
goals.property: Only the owner or an approved operator can transfer.

goals.name: no_reentrancy
goals.property: The receiver hook cannot reenter to observe inconsistent ownership.

protocols.threat_model: Adversary controls the receiver hook / operator approvals.
protocols.flaw: The onERC721Received hook enables reentrancy in naive marketplace/lending integrations (same class as ERC-777); unset/never-expiring operator approvals and approval phishing remain a major real-world loss vector.

protocols.name: ERC-721A (batch minting)
protocols.overview: ERC-721A reduces gas for sequential batch mints by tracking an ownership slot's begin timestamp; ownerOf derives ownership from the packed slot.

goals.name: ownership_correctness
goals.property: ownerOf is correct for all tokens including batch-minted ones.

goals.name: no_transfer_bypass
goals.property: Batch minting does not let an attacker claim another user's token.

protocols.threat_model: Adversary mints/transfers and probes slot-packing edge cases (e.g. minting to a contract, transfer of a first-owned token).
protocols.flaw: The packed ownership-slot optimization has had edge-case bugs around burning and transferring the first token owned by an address, where a naive implementation can report wrong ownership; these require very careful slot bookkeeping.

protocols.name: OpenSea Seaport
protocols.overview: Seaport is a marketplace protocol where orders are signed structs (offers/considerations) matched on-chain; fulfillments specify how to transfer items, and an order hash is the offer identifier.

goals.name: order_authorization
goals.property: Only orders signed by the offerer are fulfilled as specified.

goals.name: consideration_satisfaction
goals.property: All consideration items are paid before the offer is transferred.

goals.name: order_expiry
goals.property: Expired or cancelled orders cannot be fulfilled.

protocols.threat_model: Adversary crafts orders, tips, and fulfillment components; cannot forge signatures.
protocols.flaw: Order matching is extremely expressive; signature-domain confusion (e.g. counter/maker signature validity), mismatched offer/consideration tips, and unlisted consideration recipients have enabled thefts and trick users into signing orders that transfer more than expected. Social-engineering/order-hash confusion is the dominant real loss.

protocols.name: Wyvern Exchange
protocols.overview: Wyvern (early OpenSea) matches signed sell/offer orders with a delegate/registry pattern using CALL/DELEGATECALL target specifications.

goals.name: order_binding
goals.property: The executed transfer matches the signed order's target and calldata.

goals.name: no_reentrancy
goals.property: Matching cannot be reentered to double-fill an order.

protocols.threat_model: Adversary supplies crafted targets/calldata and reentrancy.
protocols.flaw: The generic CALL/DELEGATECALL order execution model was the root of the 2022 OpenSea copycat bug that let attackers steal NFTs via unvalidated calldata/initialization across fork contracts; order matching also lacked robust reentrancy/double-fill protection.

protocols.name: CryptoPunks
protocols.overview: CryptoPunks predates ERC-721: a custom market contract tracks ownership and bids, with raw transfer and offer/bid functions.

goals.name: ownership_integrity
goals.property: Ownership only changes via a valid transfer/sale.

goals.name: bid_escrow_safety
goals.property: Escrowed bids can only be withdrawn by the bidder or applied to an accepted sale.

protocols.threat_model: Adversary interacts with bid/accept methods and the fallback function.
protocols.flaw: The custom market had well-known quirks/bugs (e.g. seller-bid confusion and a function-selector clash) that let users accidentally transfer punks for free / to the contract; it is a poster child for non-standard token interfaces.

protocols.name: ERC-2981 NFT Royalties
protocols.overview: ERC-2981 exposes royaltyInfo(tokenId, salePrice) returning a receiver and amount; marketplaces are expected to honor it, but it is advisory only.

goals.name: royalty_enforcement
goals.property: A compliant sale pays the specified royalty to the receiver.

goals.name: no_royalty_bypass
goals.property: Sellers cannot avoid royalties by routing through a marketplace.

protocols.threat_model: Adversary is the seller/marketplace choosing whether to honor royaltyInfo.
protocols.flaw: The standard is advisory: on-chain enforcement is impossible without restricting transfer, so marketplaces can (and do) skip royalties or use wrapper contracts that bypass the receiver; royalty evasion is a known design limitation.

protocols.name: ERC-6551 Token-Bound Accounts
protocols.overview: ERC-6551 gives every NFT a deterministic smart-contract account controlled by the NFT's owner; the account can hold assets and execute calls.

goals.name: owner_control
goals.property: Only the current NFT owner can execute from the account.

goals.name: account_uniqueness
goals.property: The account address is deterministically bound to the NFT.

goals.name: no_cross_account_control
goals.property: Control of one account cannot affect another.

protocols.threat_model: Adversary transfers/approves the NFT and probes account ownership checks.
protocols.flaw: Account control follows the NFT, so an NFT transfer or a compromised operator approval hands over the entire bound account and all its assets; implementations that cache the owner or use ERC-721 enumerable/approval edge cases have allowed unintended control.

protocols.name: EIP-7702 Set-Code Delegation
protocols.overview: EIP-7702 lets an EOA set code (a delegation indicator) to a contract, temporarily giving the EOA smart-account behavior while retaining its key.

goals.name: delegation_authorization
goals.property: Only the EOA's key can authorize or clear a delegation.

goals.name: no_replay
goals.property: Delegation authorizations are chain- and nonce-bound and cannot be replayed.

goals.name: storage_isolation
goals.property: Delegated code cannot corrupt the EOA's storage/behavior unexpectedly.

protocols.threat_model: Adversary is a relayer or a malicious delegate contract; can replay signed authorizations.
protocols.flaw: The design expands the attack surface: signed delegation authorizations can be front-run/replayed across chains if not domain-separated, delegate contracts can execute in the EOA's context (drain via arbitrary calls), and clearing/re-delegating semantics are subtle; the standard had to add nonce/chain binding.

protocols.name: EIP-3074 AUTH/AUTHCALL
protocols.overview: EIP-3074 adds AUTH and AUTHCALL opcodes letting a sponsor (invoker) act on behalf of an EOA after an ECDSA authorization; the invoker gets full control within the call.

goals.name: authorization_binding
goals.property: The invoker can only act within the authorized scope.

goals.name: no_replay
goals.property: Authorizations are bound to chain/invoker/nonce.

protocols.threat_model: Adversary is a malicious invoker that gets temporary control of the EOA.
protocols.flaw: AUTH grants the invoker full control of the EOA for the transaction (including arbitrary calls), so any authorization to a malicious/buggy invoker drains the account; replay protection must be in the invoker, and the spec was ultimately superseded by EIP-7702 partly for these reasons.

protocols.name: Gnosis Safe Modules and Guards
protocols.overview: Safe modules can execute transactions from a Safe without the normal owner threshold; guards can veto transactions. Modules extend Safe with automation.

goals.name: module_authorization
goals.property: Only enabled modules can execute, and only within their intended scope.

goals.name: threshold_not_bypassed
goals.property: A module cannot bypass the owner threshold for arbitrary transfers.

goals.name: guard_completeness
goals.property: A guard can veto every state-changing path.

protocols.threat_model: Adversary compromises or lures the Safe into enabling a malicious module.
protocols.flaw: Enabled modules have full execution power over the Safe; a malicious or buggy module (or one enabled through a single compromised owner signature) drains all assets, bypassing the threshold. Real Safe deployments have been drained via malicious modules and via delegatecall to untrusted contracts.

protocols.name: Social Recovery Wallet
protocols.overview: A smart wallet where guardians can replace a lost signer key after a delay; the owner can cancel a pending recovery.

goals.name: recovery_authorization
goals.property: Only a quorum of current guardians can initiate recovery.

goals.name: owner_veto
goals.property: The legitimate owner can cancel an in-progress recovery before it executes.

goals.name: guardian_set_integrity
goals.property: A compromised guardian cannot shrink or replace the guardian set unilaterally.

protocols.threat_model: Adversary compromises a minority of guardians and tries to recover the wallet.
protocols.flaw: If the owner is unavailable (key lost) exactly when recovery is intended, the delay window is the only defense; a guardian quorum can steal the wallet during that window, and a compromised guardian combined with owner inactivity (or a missed veto) completes theft. Implementations have also lacked a proper guardian-set update quorum.

protocols.name: Uniswap V4 Hooks
protocols.overview: V4 uses a singleton pool manager with hooks that run before/after pool actions (initialize, swap, liquidity, donate), letting custom logic alter behavior.

goals.name: invariant_preservation
goals.property: Hooks cannot break the core constant-product accounting.

goals.name: hook_authorization
goals.property: Only the pool's registered hook can run and only for its pool.

goals.name: no_reentrancy
goals.property: Hooks cannot reenter the pool manager to corrupt state.

protocols.threat_model: Adversary deploys a malicious hook or exploits a vulnerable hook's reentrancy/flash accounting.
protocols.flaw: V4 moves a large amount of security into user-deployed hooks: a malicious/buggy hook can reenter the pool manager, mis-handle donate/fee accounting, or break the unlocked-state invariant. The attack surface is the hooks, not the core math.

protocols.name: Aave V3 E-Mode and Isolation Mode
protocols.overview: Aave V3 adds efficiency mode (higher LTV within correlated assets) and isolation mode (new assets can only be borrowed up to a debt ceiling, with limited collateral use).

goals.name: emode_soundness
goals.property: E-mode LTV is only granted to correlated assets and liquidation remains possible.

goals.name: debt_ceiling_enforcement
goals.property: Isolated assets cannot exceed their debt ceiling.

goals.name: oracle_consistency
goals.property: Price feeds are consistent across correlated assets.

protocols.threat_model: Adversary exploits correlated-asset price divergence and oracle inconsistency; may be a governance/parameter attacker.
protocols.flaw: E-mode applies high LTV assuming assets stay correlated; if the correlation breaks (a depeg or an oracle that lags one asset), positions become undercollateralized and bad debt accrues. Isolation-mode and debt-ceiling parameters are governance-controlled and can be mis-set.

protocols.name: Morpho Blue
protocols.overview: Morpho Blue is a minimal immutable lending primitive: each market is a single (collateral, loan, oracle, IRM, LLTV) tuple; positions are matched peer-to-peer with a fallback to the underlying protocol.

goals.name: market_solvency
goals.property: Positions cannot exceed the market's LLTV.

goals.name: oracle_soundness
goals.property: The market oracle cannot be manipulated to liquidate or borrow unfairly.

goals.name: no_bad_debt
goals.property: Liquidations keep markets solvent.

protocols.threat_model: Adversary manipulates a market's oracle or exploits isolated-market parameter choices.
protocols.flaw: Morpho Blue deliberately pushes risk to market creation: a permissionless market with a manipulable or non-standard oracle, exotic collateral, or bad LLTV can accrue bad debt, and immutable markets cannot be paused or upgraded. Oracle/oracle-adaptor risk is entirely on the curator/borrower.

protocols.name: Pendle Yield Tokenization
protocols.overview: Pendle splits a yield-bearing asset into a principal token (PT) and a yield token (YT); PT redeems 1:1 at maturity, YT captures yield, and an AMM trades them.

goals.name: pt_redemption_integrity
goals.property: PT redeems exactly its principal at maturity.

goals.name: yt_yield_accounting
goals.property: YT claims exactly the yield accrued over its holding period.

goals.name: amm_solvency
goals.property: The PT/YT AMM remains solvent at maturity.

protocols.threat_model: Adversary manipulates the AMM or exploits yield-accounting indexing across time.
protocols.flaw: Yield accounting with index normalisation and maturity transitions is subtle: rounding/index-seeding and flash manipulation of PT/YT AMM prices near maturity have been exploited, and malicious/rebasing yield-bearing collateral can break the PT:YT invariant.

protocols.name: GMX Perpetual Exchange
protocols.overview: GMX is a pooled-liquidity perpetual DEX: traders open leveraged positions against a GLP/GM pool, pricing comes from an oracle, and liquidators/keepers close positions.

goals.name: oracle_price_integrity
goals.property: Positions are priced only from a manipulation-resistant oracle.

goals.name: pool_solvency
goals.property: Trader PnL cannot drain the LP pool beyond design limits.

goals.name: liquidation_correctness
goals.property: Liquidations execute only when the position is undercollateralized.

protocols.threat_model: Adversary manipulates the price feed or exploits keeper/execution ordering.
protocols.flaw: The design relies on a fast, manipulation-resistant oracle; price manipulation (including through low-liquidity venues and oracle latency) has repeatedly drained perp DEXes, and keeper/execution ordering can be exploited for unfair fills.

protocols.name: Synthetix Synths and Atomic Swaps
protocols.overview: Synthetix issues synthetic assets backed by staked SNX; a debt pool tracks global debt and a shared debt distribution, and atomic swaps let users exchange synths at oracle prices.

goals.name: debt_share_correctness
goals.property: A staker's debt share reflects only protocol-wide debt changes, not another staker's trades.

goals.name: atomic_swap_fairness
goals.property: Atomic swaps are priced such that the debt pool is not drained by MEV.

goals.name: oracle_freshness
goals.property: Stale prices cannot be used to trade profitably.

protocols.threat_model: Adversary races oracle updates with atomic swaps and front-runs the debt pool.
protocols.flaw: Atomic swaps plus an oracle that updates on a schedule enable front-running/sandwiching of price updates against the shared debt pool (documented atomic-swap/front-running attacks); stale or lagged oracle prices let traders extract value from stakers.

protocols.name: Ethena USDe (delta-neutral stablecoin)
protocols.overview: USDe is backed by delta-neutral positions: staked ETH plus a short perpetual future; the funding rate and counterparty/exchange risk determine solvency, with an insurance fund and mint/redeem.

goals.name: peg_solvency
goals.property: USDe remains fully backed under funding-rate and basis moves.

goals.name: custody_safety
goals.property: Collateral held off-chain at custodians/exchanges cannot be lost or double-used.

goals.name: redemption_liveness
goals.property: USDe can be redeemed when markets are open.

protocols.threat_model: Adversary exploits exchange/custodian risk, negative funding, or a basis blowout; the protocol relies on off-chain counterparties.
protocols.flaw: Solvency depends on centralized exchanges/custodians and perpetual funding: sustained negative funding, a major exchange failure, or collateral being rehypothecated breaks backing, and redemption can be gated exactly when it is needed. This is a real trust/design exposure, not a cryptographic break.

protocols.name: EigenLayer Restaking
protocols.overview: EigenLayer lets ETH stakers opt into additional services (AVSs) with slashing conditions, re-using stake for economic security.

goals.name: slashing_completeness
goals.property: Misbehaviour defined by an AVS is slashable.

goals.name: withdrawal_safety
goals.property: Stake cannot be withdrawn while slashable obligations are open.

goals.name: no_double_slashing
goals.property: A stake cannot be slashed beyond its size across AVSs.

protocols.threat_model: Adversary is an operator/AVS colluding to avoid slashing or to slash unfairly.
protocols.flaw: Restaking creates intersubjective/cascading slashing risk: an AVS's slashing semantics may be unenforceable on-chain, operators can exit between misbehaviour and slashing (withdrawal queue design), and correlated AVS failures can slash the same stake repeatedly.

protocols.name: Pyth Network Price Oracle
protocols.overview: Pyth aggregates first-party publisher price feeds off-chain and posts them on-chain with signed updates (price, confidence, publish time); consumers pay to update and read.

goals.name: publisher_quorum
goals.property: A price is accepted only with enough publisher signatures and stake.

goals.name: staleness_detection
goals.property: Consumers can reject stale updates.

goals.name: confidence_bounds
goals.property: Consumers can account for the reported confidence interval.

protocols.threat_model: Adversary cannot compromise a publisher quorum; may exploit stale prices or confidence handling in consumers.
protocols.flaw: The signed-update aggregation is sound; losses come from consumer misuse (not checking publish time/confidence), which is an integration bug.

protocols.name: UMA Optimistic Oracle
protocols.overview: UMA lets a proposer assert an outcome with a bond; anyone can dispute within a liveness window, escalating to a token-holder vote (DVM) if disputed.

goals.name: assertion_correctness
goals.property: Only true assertions finalize.

goals.name: dispute_liveness
goals.property: An honest disputer can challenge within the window.

goals.name: dvm_soundness
goals.property: The DVM cannot be economically captured to finalize a false assertion.

protocols.threat_model: Adversary is a dishonest proposer/disputer with capital and governance tokens; may grief or capture votes.
protocols.flaw: The escalation-to-vote model is capture-prone: a large token holder can vote to finalize a false assertion, and disputers face griefing costs if the liveness/bond parameters are mis-set. UMA-dependent protocols have settled incorrect values this way.

protocols.name: Axelar General Message Passing
protocols.overview: Axelar is a PoS validator network that observes source-chain events and signs cross-chain messages executed by a gateway on the destination chain.

goals.name: message_authenticity
goals.property: A command executes only if signed by the Axelar validator quorum for the source chain.

goals.name: command_uniqueness
goals.property: A command id executes at most once.

goals.name: approval_correctness
goals.property: Token approval/transfer amounts follow the source lock/burn.

protocols.threat_model: Adversary controls <1/3 of validator stake; may exploit command-id replay or approval-encoding bugs.
protocols.flaw: Security reduces to the Axelar validator set (permissioned-ish) and the gateway's command handling; historical cross-chain gateway implementations have suffered command-id replay and approval-amount encoding bugs, and a validator-set failure is catastrophic.

protocols.name: Chainlink CCIP
protocols.overview: CCIP uses a decentralized oracle network (Committing + Executing DONs) plus optional risk management to move messages and tokens; an on-chain Router enforces lane config and rate limits.

goals.name: message_authenticity
goals.property: Execution happens only for messages attested by the oracle network.

goals.name: lane_and_rate_limit
goals.property: Per-lane rate limits and token pools are enforced.

goals.name: no_router_confusion
goals.property: Messages cannot be redirected to the wrong receiver.

protocols.threat_model: Adversary cannot corrupt the DON; exploits misconfigured lanes/receivers and rate-limit accounting.
protocols.flaw: The dual-DON + on-chain validation and rate-limit design is sound under the DON-honesty assumption; known issues are configuration (receiver/lane) mistakes rather than a protocol break.

protocols.name: Hyperlane Interchain Messaging
protocols.overview: Hyperlane is permissionless: any chain can be connected by deploying Mailbox/ISM contracts; security is provided by a configurable Interchain Security Module (ISM) per application.

goals.name: ism_verification
goals.property: A message is delivered only if the app's ISM validates it.

goals.name: ism_authorization
goals.property: The ISM cannot be replaced without authorization.

goals.name: message_uniqueness
goals.property: Messages are consumed at most once.

protocols.threat_model: Adversary is a relayer or can change/trick a weak ISM configuration.
protocols.flaw: Security is entirely the chosen ISM: multisig-ISM with a single owner or a default trusting relayer collapses to one signer, and unauthorized ISM changes let an attacker self-attest. Misconfiguration is the documented failure mode.

protocols.name: Ethereum Gasper (LMD-GHOST + FFG)
protocols.overview: Gasper combines LMD-GHOST fork choice (latest-message-driven) with Casper FFG finality; attesters vote for a head and for source/target checkpoints; slashings punish surround/equivocation.

goals.name: safety
goals.property: Conflicting checkpoints cannot be finalized without slashing.

goals.name: liveness
goals.property: With honest majority and synchrony, the chain finalizes.

goals.name: fork_choice_coherence
goals.property: LMD-GHOST does not let a minority reorg finalized history.

protocols.threat_model: Adversary controls <1/3 of stake for safety and <1/2 for liveness; may cause reorgs and balancing attacks.
protocols.flaw: LMD-GHOST has known balancing/reorg attacks in the presence of network delays and adversarial timing (documented by Neu, Tas, Gasser, Zhang et al.), and validator inactivity leaks penalize liveness; safety needs <1/3 but chain quality/MEV reorgs are exploitable below that.

protocols.name: Solana Tower BFT / Proof of History
protocols.overview: Solana orders transactions with Proof of History (a verifiable delay of hashes) and finalizes with Tower BFT, where validators lock a vote tower and vote for increasingly many slots.

goals.name: safety
goals.property: Two conflicting slots cannot both be finalized under the stake bound.

goals.name: liveness
goals.property: With enough honest stake and a healthy leader schedule, progress continues.

goals.name: poh_ordering_integrity
goals.property: PoH provides a reliable ordering/cryptographic clock.

protocols.threat_model: Adversary controls a minority of stake and can spam/congest; PoH leaders can censor.
protocols.flaw: Throughput and leader scheduling create liveness/censorship risks (the network has repeatedly halted under load), and the locked-vote tower with long lockups gives liveness and reorg concerns; PoH is an ordering aid, not a consensus-safety proof.

protocols.name: AptosBFT
protocols.overview: AptosBFT is a chained BFT consensus (HotStuff-like) with a leader reputation/pipeline and a round-based quorum certificate.

goals.name: safety
goals.property: No two correct validators commit conflicting blocks.

goals.name: liveness
goals.property: After GST a correct leader commits.

protocols.threat_model: Adversary controls <1/3 of voting power.
protocols.flaw: Derived from safe chained-BFT constructions; no protocol-level safety break known under <1/3 Byzantine.

protocols.name: Sui Narwhal/Bullshark
protocols.overview: Sui separates data dissemination (Narwhal mempool DAG) from ordering (Bullshark BFT), giving high throughput with causal-order certificates.

goals.name: safety
goals.property: Validators agree on a total order of committed certificates.

goals.name: liveness
goals.property: With a correct leader and GST, commits proceed.

protocols.threat_model: Adversary controls <1/3 of stake and may be a leader in some rounds.
protocols.flaw: No known safety flaw under <1/3 Byzantine; DAG-based constructions provide the standard BFT guarantees.

protocols.name: Polkadot GRANDPA Finality
protocols.overview: GRANDPA finalizes chains (not blocks) by having validators vote on the best chain containing a set of blocks, with a supermajority and a multi-round protocol.

goals.name: safety
goals.property: Two finalized chains never conflict.

goals.name: liveness
goals.property: Finality progresses with >2/3 honest validators.

protocols.threat_model: Adversary controls <1/3 of stake (and performs the accountable-fault attribution otherwise).
protocols.flaw: GRANDPA is designed for accountable safety and is secure under <1/3 Byzantine; no known safety break.

protocols.name: Filecoin Expected Consensus
protocols.overview: Filecoin uses storage-based leader election (ElectionProof) weighted by quality-adjusted power, a tipset structure, and a longest-chain rule over tipsets.

goals.name: chain_quality
goals.property: Adversarial mining power cannot outpace honest chain growth.

goals.name: storage_proof_binding
goals.property: Power derives from valid PoRep/PoSt proofs.

protocols.threat_model: Adversary with a minority of storage power and rational miners.
protocols.flaw: Security depends on the honest storage-power majority and correct quality-adjusted power accounting; flaws in power accounting or proof verification (e.g. snapshot/proof bugs) let an adversary gain outsized influence, and rational withholding can reorg.

protocols.name: Bulletproofs Range Proofs
protocols.overview: Bulletproofs are short non-interactive zero-knowledge range proofs without a trusted setup, used in Confidential Transactions to prove a value is in [0, 2^n).

goals.name: range_soundness
goals.property: No prover can prove a value outside the range.

goals.name: zero_knowledge
goals.property: The proof reveals nothing beyond the range statement.

goals.name: binding
goals.property: Commitments/transcripts bind the proven value.

protocols.threat_model: Adversary is a malicious prover; no toxic waste exists.
protocols.flaw: Sound and transparent (no setup); security reduces to the discrete-log and Fiat-Shamir assumptions, with implementation care on aggregation/transcript binding.

protocols.name: Halo2 / Recursive Proofs
protocols.overview: Halo2 uses an inner-product polynomial commitment with no trusted setup and supports recursive proof composition, used in Zcash Orchard and zkEVMs.

goals.name: soundness
goals.property: A false statement has no valid proof.

goals.name: commitment_binding
goals.property: The commitment scheme binds the polynomial.

goals.name: transcript_binding
goals.property: Fiat-Shamir challenges are uniquely determined.

protocols.threat_model: Adversary is a malicious prover; no setup trust required.
protocols.flaw: No soundness flaw in the construction; the historical Orchard counterfeiting bug was an implementation/transcript issue, not a break of Halo2.

protocols.name: Nova (folding scheme IVC)
protocols.overview: Nova is an incrementally verifiable computation scheme based on a relaxed R1CS folding scheme and a cycle of elliptic curves; it avoids per-step SNARKs.

goals.name: ivc_validity
goals.property: A final proof attests to the correctness of the entire computation chain.

goals.name: folding_soundness
goals.property: Each fold preserves the satisfiability relation.

protocols.threat_model: Adversary is a malicious prover.
protocols.flaw: Sound under the commitment/FS assumptions; risks are implementation-level (curve cycle/comparison correctness).

protocols.name: Recursive SNARK / proof aggregation
protocols.overview: Recursive SNARKs verify a proof inside another proof, enabling aggregation and incrementally verifiable computation across many steps.

goals.name: composition_soundness
goals.property: The outer proof is sound if the inner verifier is correctly embedded.

goals.name: domain_binding
goals.property: Each recursion level binds the correct verification key/domain.

protocols.threat_model: Adversary is a malicious prover exploiting a missing binding in the recursive verifier.
protocols.flaw: Incorrectly embedding the inner verification key, public inputs, or domain separator in the recursive circuit lets a prover fork/replay proofs across contexts; recursive-circuit bugs are a documented source of counterfeiting (e.g. the Zcash Orchard incident).

protocols.name: RISC Zero zkVM
protocols.overview: A general-purpose zkVM that proves execution of RISC-V programs and issues a receipt bound to an image id and journal (public outputs).

goals.name: execution_soundness
goals.property: A receipt is accepted only for a faithful execution of the claimed program image.

goals.name: image_journal_binding
goals.property: The receipt binds the exact image id and public journal.

goals.name: no_forged_receipt
goals.property: An attacker cannot forge a receipt without executing the program.

protocols.threat_model: Adversary is a malicious prover/dApp reusing receipts across contexts.
protocols.flaw: The proof system is sound, but dApps must bind the image id and journal to the intended context: accepting a receipt without checking the image id, or reusing a journal across different contracts, lets an attacker replay a valid receipt for an unrelated action.

protocols.name: CoW Protocol (batch auctions)
protocols.overview: CoW Protocol batches user orders and settles them with a uniform clearing price via solvers; orders are signed intents and the CoW settlement contract enforces interactions.

goals.name: uniform_clearing_price
goals.property: All matched orders in a batch clear at the same price per token pair.

goals.name: user_limit_respected
goals.property: No order settles worse than its signed limit price.

goals.name: solver_bond_safety
goals.property: A malicious solver cannot steal user funds beyond its bond.

protocols.threat_model: Adversary is a solver choosing interactions and batch composition.
protocols.flaw: Solver-controlled arbitrary interactions and partially fillable/limit order semantics are a large surface: a malicious/buggy solver can craft interactions that violate the intended uniform-price outcome or drain allowances (mitigated by bonds/simulation), and order-signing interface attacks have caused real losses.

protocols.name: EIP-712 Typed Structured Data Hashing
protocols.overview: EIP-712 defines a hashing/signing scheme for structured data with a domain separator (name, version, chainId, verifyingContract) and type hashes.

goals.name: domain_separation
goals.property: A signature is valid only for the exact domain (chain + contract).

goals.name: struct_binding
goals.property: The signature binds the exact field values and type.

goals.name: no_replay
goals.property: Signatures cannot be replayed across domains or nonces.

protocols.threat_model: Adversary replays signatures across chains/contracts or trick users into signing ambiguous payloads.
protocols.flaw: The scheme is only as safe as its use: domains that omit chainId/verifyingContract are cross-domain replayable; nested structs without type hashes, or ambiguous field ordering, enable signature-confusion attacks; wallets often display insufficient detail, enabling blind-signing theft.

protocols.name: EIP-1271 Contract Signatures
protocols.overview: EIP-1271 lets a contract validate a signature via isValidSignature(hash, signature), enabling smart-contract accounts (Safe, AA wallets) to sign.

goals.name: signature_validation_soundness
goals.property: isValidSignature returns the magic value only for genuinely authorized signatures.

goals.name: reentrancy_safety
goals.property: Verification cannot be used to reenter the verifier.

goals.name: replay_binding
goals.property: The signed hash is bound to the intended action/domain.

protocols.threat_model: Adversary is a malicious contract signer returning the magic value, or a relayer exploiting reentrancy during verification.
protocols.flaw: The standard is stateful and can be reentered: a malicious contract signer can return the magic value while reentering the verifier, and verifiers that ignore the returned magic value or verify outside the intended domain accept invalid signatures. Real NFT/marketplace exploits abused ERC-1271 verification.

protocols.name: secp256r1 / Passkey Smart Accounts
protocols.overview: Smart accounts verify WebAuthn/passkey signatures over secp256r1 (P-256), often via an on-chain P-256 verifier precompile or contract and a ReplaySafeHash domain.

goals.name: key_binding
goals.property: Only the registered passkey public key can authorize actions.

goals.name: domain_binding
goals.property: Signatures are bound to the account and chain.

goals.name: verifier_soundness
goals.property: The P-256 verifier rejects malformed signatures.

protocols.threat_model: Adversary replays WebAuthn assertions or exploits a malformed-signature acceptance bug in the verifier.
protocols.flaw: Passkey assertions are not chain/account bound by default, so accounts must wrap them in a replay-safe hash; naive P-256 verifiers accept non-canonical/malleable inputs or fail to hash the challenge correctly, enabling replay across accounts or signature forgery.

protocols.name: Tornado Cash Mixer
protocols.overview: A fixed-denomination mixer: users deposit into a Merkle tree and later withdraw to a fresh address using a zk-SNARK proving membership of a note, with a nullifier preventing double withdrawal.

goals.name: withdrawal_once
goals.property: A note can be withdrawn at most once (nullifier binding).

goals.name: anonymity_set
goals.property: The withdrawer is unlinkable to the depositor within the anonymity set.

goals.name: deposit_withdraw_consistency
goals.property: Only notes inserted into the tree can be withdrawn.

protocols.threat_model: Adversary is an observer/relayer; may exploit note leakage, relayer front-running, or metadata.
protocols.flaw: The cryptography is sound, but anonymity is easily broken by metadata (address reuse, relayer choice, gas/amount timing) and the verifier historically accepted non-canonical proofs (the 2021 tornado.cash bug where the nullifier check could be bypassed for one pool via a malformed proof). Also compliance/sanctions are external.

protocols.name: ENS Name Registry
protocols.overview: ENS assigns names via a registrar that commits/reveals to prevent front-running; a registry maps names to owners/resolvers, and a resolver records addresses.

goals.name: name_ownership_uniqueness
goals.property: A name has one owner, transferable only by the owner.

goals.name: commit_reveal_fairness
goals.property: An observer cannot front-run a registration by copying the reveal.

goals.name: resolver_authorization
goals.property: Records can be changed only by the name owner/authorized controller.

protocols.threat_model: Adversary front-runs registration and resolver updates.
protocols.flaw: The commit-reveal scheme has historically been bypassed/raced (commitments are only weakly bound to the registrant, and reveal front-running/griefing is possible); name-wrapper and resolver-controller permissions have allowed unauthorized record changes and takeover in misconfigured setups.

protocols.name: Curve veCRV Vote-Buying / bribe markets
protocols.overview: Curve locks CRV for veCRV to direct emissions to gauges; bribe markets (e.g. Convex/Votium) let others pay for votes, and Convex aggregates veCRV for voting power.

goals.name: vote_binding
goals.property: Locked votes cannot be double-counted or replayed after delegation.

goals.name: gauge_emission_correctness
goals.property: Emissions follow the recorded vote weights.

goals.name: no_flash_governance
goals.property: Voting power cannot be obtained flash-loan-like for a single epoch.

protocols.threat_model: Adversary acquires voting power atomically or exploits vote-delegation/accounting.
protocols.flaw: The design is explicitly vote-market friendly, which enables governance capture by capital and makes flash-loaned/borrowed voting power profitable in edge cases; vote-escrow accounting and delegation bugs have allowed double-voting or misdirected emissions.

protocols.name: MEV-Boost Relay
protocols.overview: A relay receives builder bids and payloads, validates them, and passes the winning header to the proposer; the relay is a trusted party between builders and proposers.

goals.name: payload_availability
goals.property: The proposer can obtain the full payload after signing the header.

goals.name: bid_integrity
goals.property: The relay does not leak the payload before the proposal or alter bids.

goals.name: equivocation_prevention
goals.property: The relay cannot serve conflicting views to proposers.

protocols.threat_model: Adversary is a malicious relay or a network attacker; relays are permissioned-ish and few.
protocols.flaw: The relay is a trusted central party: a malicious relay can withhold payloads (causing missed slots), leak builder intents for unbundling, or equivocate; relay outages have caused mass missed proposals. This is a real centralization/availability flaw.

protocols.name: ERC-3156 Flash Loans
protocols.overview: ERC-3156 standardizes flash loans: a lender transfers assets to a borrower, calls onFlashLoan, and requires repayment plus fee before the transaction ends.

goals.name: repayment_atomicity
goals.property: The transaction reverts unless principal plus fee is repaid.

goals.name: no_balance_manipulation
goals.property: A flash loan cannot leave the lender with fewer assets.

goals.name: initiator_binding
goals.property: The callback verifies the caller is the trusted lender.

protocols.threat_model: Adversary is a borrower with arbitrary callback code and atomic composability.
protocols.flaw: Flash loans are a feature, but receivers that do not verify msg.sender against the expected lender (or that use transfer instead of safeTransfer) can be reentered by a malicious 'lender' or have their allowance drained; the pattern has been the primitive in many DeFi drains.

protocols.name: ERC-6909 Minimal Multi-Token
protocols.overview: ERC-6909 is a minimal multi-token interface with per-id balances and operator approvals, separate from ERC-1155.

goals.name: balance_integrity
goals.property: Per-id balances are conserved across transfers.

goals.name: operator_authorization
goals.property: Only approved operators can move tokens.

goals.name: allowance_correctness
goals.property: Per-id allowances are enforced and not shared across ids.

protocols.threat_model: Adversary exploits per-id allowance/operator confusion.
protocols.flaw: Multi-token operators and per-id allowances are easy to confuse: implementations that share an approval across ids, or that fail to decrement infinite allowances correctly, let an operator drain unintended ids. Interface- confusion with ERC-1155/ERC-20 is a recurring integration risk.
